module.name: Coaching Julie — Monday to Saturday
module.description: A week-long journey, a small daily challenge and a quiz to anchor the concepts, to make real progress on your topic.

exercice.objectif: Spot a situation where your voice wasn't heard enough, and prepare a simple sentence to make it heard next time.
Put that sentence into practice in a meeting or exchange, and observe the reaction you get.
Identify a task you could delegate today, and actually delegate it.
Ask a colleague or someone close to you for constructive feedback on your posture this week.
Note down a success from the week, however small, and share it with someone.

bilan.description: Saturday review: a synthesis of the week (exercises + quiz), then the choice between going deeper with your e-Coach (redo the questions you got wrong) or being connected.

module.name: Self-Promotion and Personal Branding Test
module.description: Sharing your achievements and openly highlighting the impact of your work.

exercice.objectif: Inventory of Unrecognized Achievements : Identify and quantify your actual, undocumented contributions. Take 15 minutes to review your activities over the past 6 months. Identify 5 successes or problems solved that were not included in your original job description. For each item, assign an impact metric (e.g., time saved, budget preserved, streamlined process, customer/team satisfaction). Include these 5 items in your annual summary report or impact log.

The “Impact Matrix” Pitch : Transform an operational task into a narrative of executive value. Select an operational task that you perform regularly. Restate it using the following structure: [Optimization Action] + [Process Transformation] = [Strategic/Financial Outcome]. Write a 30-second verbal pitch and practice delivering it aloud until it flows smoothly and naturally.

Anchoring and Amplifying in Meetings : To secure ownership of your ideas and dominate the verbal space. Before your next key meeting, identify a major idea or recommendation you wish to bring forward. Craft a direct anchoring statement (e.g., “Based on data from my division, here is the decision I recommend...” ). Make a prior agreement with a trusted colleague: practice building on each other’s comments using reinforcement phrases (e.g., “I reaffirm the key point raised by [Name]...” ).

The Salary “Fact Sheet” Simulation : Prepare for a salary negotiation based on tangible data. Create a one-page document (“Fact Sheet”) summarizing your top 3 contributions of the year along with their financial or operational metrics. Determine your target figure based on market benchmarks. Conduct a 10-minute role-play with a peer or coach to practice stating this figure without hesitation, then handling the silence that follows.

Mapping Your Sponsors : To structure your network of influence and find strategic allies. List three executives or decision-makers outside your direct reporting line who hold significant influence within the organization. For each one, identify an area of expertise where you can seek their advice or share a recent strategic achievement. Plan to reach out or have an informal interaction with at least one of them within the next 14 days.

question.text: During your annual review, your manager praises your commitment. Which statement best acknowledges your work?

options.option: Thank you, thats kind of you, but its really the whole teams hard work that paid off.
I restructured the sales strategy, which led to a 15% increase in sales.
Yes, I was lucky to have some good projects this year.
I just followed the roadmap I was given.

question.explication: Answer B directly links personal action to a measurable result (15%). Excessive modesty (answer A) or attributing success to chance (answer C) downplay personal merit and minimize the perceived value of the work.

question.text: A colleague takes credit for the key idea you presented in a meeting last week. What do you do?

options.option: You say nothing at the time to avoid conflict and complain later in private.
You speak up immediately: Glad to see youre building on the analysis I presented on Tuesday.
You abruptly interrupt them, calling them an idea thief.
You wait until the annual review to settle the score.

question.explication: Response B publicly reassigns ownership of the idea diplomatically and firmly, without being aggressive. Letting it slide validates the other person’s appropriation, while aggression undermines your professional presence.

question.text: A director praises the quality of your presentation. What is the most appropriate response?

options.option: It was nothing at all; its a very simple topic.
Sorry about the few typos in the slides.
Thank you. I put a lot of work into structuring these analyses and clarifying the roadmap.
My colleague did most of the work.

question.explication: Accepting a compliment by acknowledging the effort and value created reinforces your credibility. Trying to apologize or downplay the work sends the message that the skills you used aren’t worth anything.

question.text: You resolved a major technical issue on an urgent basis. How do you describe this in your summary?

options.option: I simply handled the departments usual emergencies.
Crisis management that ensured service continuity for €100k in revenue.
I had to work late into the night to correct other peoples mistakes.
I fixed a bug that should never have happened.

question.explication: An emergency situation should be translated into financial or operational value preserved. This transforms a reactive task into a demonstration of business impact.

question.text: What personal tool should you maintain regularly to prepare your self-assessment?

options.option: A list of complaints about the companys shortcomings.
A weekly impact log documenting successes, key metrics, and positive feedback received.
An accurate record of your hours spent in the office.
A compilation of mistakes made by your peers.

question.explication: Memory is selective, and the recency bias causes us to forget achievements from earlier in the year. Recording facts and metrics as they occur ensures an unassailable, fact-based record during performance reviews.

question.text: Why is the statement “I was lucky to succeed on this project” counterproductive?

options.option: It shows that you are a humble and well-liked person.
Because it undermines the speakers skills and attributes success to chance.
It prompts the manager to cut the budget for the next project.
It is not harmful; it is a normal polite expression.

question.explication: Attributing one’s successes to luck undermines one’s professional credibility. If success is due to chance, the company has no strategic interest in promoting or advancing that person.

question.text: How should you present a failure or mistake in your performance review without undermining your value?

options.option: Completely hide the incident and hope no one notices.
Blame the team or external service providers.
Explain the problem encountered, the corrective actions taken, and the key lessons learned.
Apologize repeatedly while acknowledging a lack of competence.

question.explication: The ability to analyze a failure, draw lessons from it, and implement corrective measures demonstrates a high level of maturity and leadership.

question.text: What does the “modest self-deprecation” effect—often observed in women in the workplace—mean?

options.option: A negotiation technique based on offering a discount.
The tendency to downplay ones accomplishments for fear of appearing arrogant or pretentious.
Accepting a pay cut during a crisis.
A method of accounting for assets.

question.explication: Socialization often leads to a fear that assertiveness will be perceived as arrogance. This fear leads to the systematic underestimation of one’s performance.

question.text: When is the best time to publicize the success of a major project?

options.option: Only after 12 months, during the annual review.
As soon as a major milestone is reached, by sharing an impact summary or an interim report.
Never; management will notice it on its own.
During coffee breaks, informally and confidentially.

question.explication: Visibility is built in the present. Waiting until the annual review is too late and deprives the person of immediate recognition for the milestones achieved.

question.text: MONDAY’S PRACTICAL EXERCISE: You’re creating your “Impact Report.” Which of the following should NOT be included?

options.option: Financial gains or efficiency improvements generated.
An exhaustive list of all your daily, repetitive tasks.
Testimonials of satisfaction from clients or key partners.
Cross-functional projects youve led.

question.explication: An Impact Report is a valuable strategic document, not a job description. Burying achievements under operational tasks obscures the real impact and hinders executive readability. ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- --- TUESDAY: TRANSLATING YOUR WORK INTO METRICS AND BUSINESS IMPACT --------------------------------------------------------------------------------

question.text: You optimized an internal process. How would you present this success?

options.option: I changed the way we file documents in the department.
I saved 4 hours per week on document processing, which I reallocated to customer follow-up.
I finally cleaned up the mess left by my predecessor.
The work was taking too long, so I found a shortcut.

question.explication: The value lies not in the cosmetic change, but in the resources freed up (4 hours/week) and their strategic reinvestment (customer follow-up).

question.text: How can you transform a “qualitative” project (e.g., workplace well-being) into data demonstrating business impact?

options.option: By simply stating that the teams are happier.
By measuring the decrease in turnover rate (-8%) and the increase in the engagement score.
By showing photos of the events organized.
By saying that its a project that cant be measured with numbers.

question.explication: Any qualitative project can be evaluated using indirect indicators (proxies) such as retention rates, hiring, or absenteeism, which are immediately understandable to an executive committee.

question.text: During a budget planning meeting, which metric should you highlight?

options.option: The number of unpaid overtime hours youve worked.
The return on investment (ROI) and the net margin generated by your projects.
The cost of your business travel.
The difficulty of the work performed.

question.explication: The language of the executive committee is that of profitability and capital. Promoting yourself based on hardship or time spent (overtime) is ineffective compared to generating gross margin.

question.text: What should you do if you don’t have precise figures on the impact of your work?

options.option: Make up spectacular figures to make a good impression.
Dont mention any results and talk only about your motivation.
Develop a realistic estimate based on documented assumptions and orders of magnitude.
State that measuring results is not your responsibility.

question.explication: In the executive world, a well-documented estimate based on clear assumptions is better than a complete lack of metrics, which implies a lack of results-orientation.

question.text: What is the best way to title a successful project on your internal resume?

options.option: Participated in CRM meetings.
Led the CRM migration: 0 service interruptions and +12% sales productivity.
Provided support to the IT team.
Managed IT change.

question.explication: The title should combine the responsibility assumed (“Led”), risk management (“zero downtime”), and the direct impact on the company (“12% increase in productivity”).

question.text: Why is it risky to describe yourself solely as a “reliable and organized” person?

options.option: Because it shows that you lack empathy.
Because it confines you to the role of an irreplaceable but unpromotable executor.
Because these are seen as flaws in a business setting.
Because managers dont like organization.

question.explication: Reliability is perceived as a basic execution skill. If you become indispensable to day-to-day operations, your management will have an incentive to keep you in your current position rather than promote you to the C-suite.

question.text: How should you present an efficiency gain achieved through task automation?

options.option: I no longer do anything manually in this area.
Automation of reporting: elimination of 10 hours of manual reporting and reallocation of time to strategic analysis.
I found a cool piece of software that does the work for me.
The manual work was too tedious.

question.explication: The value does not come from eliminating the work, but from shifting time from execution to high-value-added activities (strategic analysis).

question.text: Which metric should you use to evaluate a customer portfolio retention initiative?

options.option: The number of empathy emails sent.
The customer retention rate (95%) and the preserved customer lifetime value (LTV).
How polite customers are during phone calls.
The time spent on courtesy meetings.

question.explication: Retention and Lifetime Value (LTV) metrics reflect high-quality relationships that safeguard recurring revenue.

question.text: You have trained three employees. How do you measure the value of this HR contribution?

options.option: I wasted three days re-explaining the basics to the new hires.
Skill development for three junior employees: achieved autonomy in one month and reduced onboarding time by 50%.
I was very kind to the new team.
I did HRs job for them.

question.explication: Training people becomes a successful HR initiative when the time to autonomy is reduced, leading to an overall increase in productivity.

question.text: TUESDAY’S PRACTICAL EXERCISE: In the “Impact Matrix,” how would you categorize the task “Organizing meetings”?

options.option: Managing room reservations and ordering meals.
Strategic alignment of decision-makers: reducing decision-making time by 2 weeks on key projects.
Taking notes and sending out meeting minutes.
Facilitating discussions and taking attendance.

question.explication: The logistical organization of a meeting is an operational task. Its strategic objective and real impact lie in facilitating decision-making and aligning stakeholders. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- WEDNESDAY: GROUNDING, ASSERTIVENESS, AND PRESENCE IN MEETINGS --------------------------------------------------------------------------------

question.text: During a meeting, a male colleague consistently cuts you off. How do you react?

options.option: You immediately fall silent and drop your point.
You raise your voice to shout over his.
You calmly resume speaking: Thomas, let me finish my point before you respond.
You leave the meeting room in protest.

question.explication: Responding calmly but firmly by addressing the interruption by name helps set clear boundaries and assert your authority without coming across as emotional.

question.text: What is the best strategy for speaking at the start of a strategic meeting?

options.option: Wait until the end of the session to express your overall opinion.
Speak up within the first 10 minutes with a structured question or statement.
Speak only if the chair calls on you by name.
Speak nonstop to monopolize the floor.

question.explication: Speaking up early establishes your presence in the discussion and cements your status as an active contributor, reducing the risk of being sidelined later on.

question.text: What does the “Amplification” technique involve to counter “Bropropriation”?

options.option: Speaking louder than everyone else in the room.
Teaming up with a colleague to publicly repeat and reattribute ideas raised by women.
Using a microphone or very large visual aids.
Sending multiple follow-up emails after meetings.

question.explication: Amplification is a collective strategy in which allies take up an idea proposed by a woman while citing her name (e.g., “As Sarah pointed out…”), thereby securing the authorship and visibility of the contribution.

question.text: How should you frame a strategic idea so that it has maximum impact during a meeting?

options.option: Im no expert, but it seems to me that perhaps…
My recommendation is to implement Option B in order to secure our 15% margin.
This is a bit of a crazy idea that you probably wont like.
If no one has any other suggestions, we could possibly try this.

question.explication: Self-deprecating preambles (“I’m no expert…”) undermine credibility before the idea is even heard. A direct statement backed by financial reasoning speaks for itself.

question.text: What should you do if you’re automatically assigned the role of “meeting secretary” (taking notes)?

options.option: Accept it without saying anything at every meeting to avoid conflict.
Suggest a rotation: I took the minutes last week; its Marcs turn today.
Refuse outright, saying its not part of your responsibilities.
Take notes in an illegible manner so you wont be asked to do it again.

question.explication: Note-taking that isn’t assigned fairly is a form of invisible “office housework.” Suggesting a rotation makes the entire group accountable.

question.text: What body language do you use at a board meeting to assert your presence?

options.option: Make yourself as small as possible and cross your arms under the table.
Rest your forearms on the table, sit up straight, and fully occupy your workspace.
Slump in your chair in a detached manner.
Keep your head down, focused on your personal notes.

question.explication: Nonverbal communication influences the perception of authority. Taking up physical space by resting your arms on the table sends a clear signal of legitimacy and commitment.

question.text: How should you respond to a personal attack or an inappropriate challenge during a meeting?

options.option: Respond with an equivalent insult.
Defend yourself in a confused and emotional manner.
Immediately refocus on the facts: Lets stick to the projects hard data so we can move forward.
Start crying due to stress.

question.explication: Directing the speaker back to the facts or metrics neutralizes the ad hominem aggression and replaces the emotional tone with professional rigor.

question.text: Why is it not recommended to start sentences with “Sorry, but…”?

options.option: Because its a grammatical error.
Because it puts the speaker in a position of being at fault before shes even made her case.
Because the word sorry is reserved for private life.
It has no impact on the audience.

question.explication: A preemptive apology diminishes the value of what is about to be said and leads the audience to look for problems in the upcoming remarks, rather than focusing on the proposal.

question.text: How should you react when a supervisor publicly credits you with a team achievement?

options.option: Ignore it and take 100% of the credit for yourself.
Thank them warmly and then specify the specific contribution of each key team member.
Correct the superior in front of everyone by saying they were wrong.
Say that you did almost nothing and that the team did it all.

question.explication: A great leader knows how to take ownership of overall success while distributing credit to the teams. This demonstrates a high level of strategic presence and managerial generosity.

question.text: WEDNESDAY PRACTICE EXERCISE: What opening statement should you prepare for the meeting?

options.option: I apologize in advance for my lack of preparation...
Based on my divisions analyses, here is the strategic direction we need to approve.
This is just my personal opinion; do with it what you will.
I dont want to waste your time, but...

question.explication: An effective opening statement is grounded in operational legitimacy (data from your division) and sets out a clear direction for approval. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- THURSDAY: SALARY NEGOTIATIONS AND FINANCIAL RECOGNITION --------------- -----------------------------------------------------------------

question.text: During your salary review, your manager mentions budget constraints. What do you say?

options.option: Oh, okay, I understand. Well talk about it again next year, then.
I understand the situation. Lets look at the value Ive created through my projects and set a timeline for six months from now.
If thats the case, Im quitting right now.
Thats not my problem; I want my raise right now.

question.explication: Insisting on an immediate refusal shuts down the negotiation. Postponing the request to an intermediate timeline and reaffirming the value you’ve created keeps the door open and engages the manager.

question.text: What is the golden rule for setting your salary expectation when you’re promoted?

options.option: Ask for what you need to cover your personal expenses.
Base your request on industry market research and aim for the top of the range to leave room for negotiation.
Accept HRs first financial offer without discussion.
Ask for the same salary as your lowest-paid colleague.

question.explication: Professional negotiation is based on the market value of the position and your profile (benchmarks), not on personal needs. Aiming for the top of the range leaves room for negotiation.

question.text: You’re offered a major new project without a promotion or a pay raise. How do you respond?

options.option: Thank you very much, Im honored that you thought of me!
Im delighted by this vote of confidence. Lets define the associated objectives and the conditions for a review in six months.
Thats unpaid work; I categorically refuse.
Ill only do it if you give me a bigger office.

question.explication: Accepting additional responsibilities without securing the possibility of a future financial review leads to an unrewarded workload.

question.text: How do you prepare a case for requesting additional financial resources or staff?

options.option: By emphasizing your current level of fatigue and stress.
By demonstrating that this investment will unlock new opportunities for profitable growth.
By pointing out that other departments have already received new hires.
By threatening to compromise the quality of your work if you dont get what you want.

question.explication: Decision-makers think in terms of return on investment (ROI). A request framed in terms of strategic and financial gains will always carry more weight than a complaint about workload.

question.text: What is the impact of the statement “I’d already be very happy if I were granted 5%”?

options.option: It shows that you are reasonable and easy to work with.
It gives your counterpart permission to offer you the absolute minimum—or even less.
It encourages management to grant you 10% out of goodwill.
It has no impact on the outcome of the negotiation.

question.explication: Stating your threshold for dissatisfaction or a minimum amount as a “wish” weakens your opening position and serves as a low anchor for the other party in the negotiation.

question.text: How should you handle an awkward silence from your manager after you’ve announced your salary request?

options.option: Fill the silence by immediately lowering your salary request.
Maintain a calm and confident demeanor while silently waiting for your counterparts response.
Apologize for asking for such a high amount.
Talk about the weather to lighten the mood.

question.explication: Silence is a classic tool for applying psychological pressure in negotiations. Giving in to the discomfort of silence by lowering your demands before even receiving a formal response is a strategic mistake.

question.text: In negotiations, what components of the overall compensation package should not be overlooked?

options.option: Only the fixed monthly gross salary.
The fixed portion, the variable portion, bonuses, the training budget, flexibility, and benefits in kind.
Verbal praise from management.
Only the title listed on the business card.

question.explication: When the fixed budget is locked in, the total value can be negotiated through variable pay, training, working conditions, or other ancillary benefits.

question.text: Your manager denies your promotion, saying, “You don’t have enough of an internal network yet.” What do you do?

options.option: Take the comment as a definitive rejection and give up.
Ask for specific criteria: What action plan can we set to build influence over the next 6 months?
Say that networking is useless and that only hard work matters.
Accuse the manager of playing favorites.

question.explication: Turning a vague objection (“lack of a network”) into a measurable action plan with a deadline forces the manager to commit to objective evaluation criteria.

question.text: What is the correct response to the argument, “Now is not the right time, given the current crisis”?

options.option: Immediately withdraw any request.
Demonstrate how your work has actually helped protect results during the crisis.
Say that the crisis doesnt exist and that its a lie.
Demand a double raise to compensate for the loss.

question.explication: In times of economic uncertainty, employees who protect profit margins, secure clients, or reduce risks are even more valuable.

question.text: THURSDAY PRACTICE EXERCISE: During a simulated salary negotiation, what is your first move?

options.option: Ask what the company plans to offer you without mentioning a specific figure.
Present your Fact Sheet demonstrating the financial value youve generated and set your anchor figure.
Say that youre underpaid compared to your colleagues.
Justify your request based on your personal loan payments.

question.explication: Setting the anchor first by backing it up with facts (Fact Sheet) establishes the starting point for the entire salary negotiation. ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- ---- FRIDAY: STRATEGIC NETWORKING, SPONSORSHIP, AND SOCIAL CAPITAL --------------------------------------------------------------------------------

question.text: What is the definition of a “sponsor” in a corporate setting compared to a simple “mentor”?

options.option: A mentor pays for your travel expenses; a sponsor proofreads your resume.
A mentor provides strategic advice; a sponsor uses their political capital to get you appointed.
There is no difference between a mentor and a sponsor.
A sponsor must be your direct manager.

question.explication: Mentoring develops expertise behind the scenes; sponsorship unlocks opportunities in the public eye. A sponsor is a leader who speaks highly of you behind closed doors where decisions are made.

question.text: How should you respond if an informal network of decision-makers (“Boys Club”) seems inaccessible to you?

options.option: Try to participate in their personal activities even if you dont enjoy them.
Identify strategic nodes of influence and create opportunities for professional exchanges on topics within your area of expertise.
Openly criticize this group in front of all employees.
Stay isolated in your office while waiting for attitudes to change.

question.explication: Bypassing the informal network requires building your own valuable network based on professional expertise, strategic content contributions, and aligned professional interests.

question.text: What is the ideal frequency for sharing a high-impact update with your internal network?

options.option: Every day via a detailed email.
In a targeted manner, during key milestones or via a value-added quarterly summary.
Once every 5 years when changing positions.
Only if management explicitly asks you to.

question.explication: Communicating too frequently leads to information overload, while communicating too infrequently makes you invisible. A quarterly update strikes the right balance of visibility.

question.text: How can you share a personal success on LinkedIn without coming across as narcissistic?

options.option: Im the best in my field, and Ive crushed the competition yet again.
Focus the post on learning, challenges overcome, and thank your teammates.
Post a photo of your pay stub.
Say that the success was easy and effortless.

question.explication: Successful self-promotion on professional networks uses educational approaches (sharing lessons learned) and collective recognition to make success inspiring and legitimate.

question.text: What should you do if a colleague tries to publicly downplay the impact of your work in front of a manager?

options.option: Insult them to defend your honor.
Calmly restate the facts using the exact impact figures validated by management.
Lower your head and nod in agreement.
Cancel the presentation and leave the room.

question.explication: Refuting an attempt to downplay your work with validated figures and facts disarms the attacker without entering into a personal conflict, thereby preserving your executive standing.

question.text: What does the “cross-sponsorship” strategy among women leaders entail?

options.option: Lending each other office supplies.
Mutually committing to cite and recommend each others skills in decision-making circles.
Writing each others reports in secret.
Taking vacation on the same dates.

question.explication: Cross-sponsorship helps create a critical mass of influence. Recommending another woman’s expertise strengthens the credibility of the entire network.

question.text: How should you approach a high-level executive to turn them into a potential sponsor?

options.option: Send them an email asking, Would you like to be my sponsor?
Ask for their opinion on a specific strategic project in which their expertise is recognized.
Wait for them at the parking lot exit to approach them.
Send them a list of all your salary demands.

question.explication: A sponsorship relationship cannot be forced. It is built gradually by engaging the executive on a specific professional issue, allowing them to see the value of your insights.

question.text: What is the one pitfall you must absolutely avoid during internal networking sessions?

options.option: Prepare in advance the topics you want to discuss.
Talk only with close colleagues from your own team.
Talk with people from departments other than your own.
Get the contact information of the people you meet to stay in touch.

question.explication: Staying in your comfort zone by interacting only with your close circle defeats the purpose of networking, which is to expand your visibility and social capital across other departments.

question.text: How can you turn an informal compliment received at the coffee machine into a career booster?

options.option: Smile, say thank you, and forget about it right away.
Politely ask the person in writing if you can include their feedback in your quarterly report.
Repeat it to everyone insistently.
Tell the person they should have given you that compliment during an official meeting.

question.explication: Formalizing informal positive feedback in writing helps build social proof that can be leveraged during performance reviews and promotion negotiations.

question.text: FRIDAY PRACTICE EXERCISE: What is the first step in mapping out your sponsors?

options.option: Send a general message to the entire company.
List the three people in management who have decision-making authority and are familiar with your results.
Wait for the next company reorganization.
Ask your close colleagues to vote for you.

question.explication: Mapping begins with clarifying the centers of power. Identifying key decision-makers allows you to focus your relational energy where the strategic impact will be greatest.

bilan.description: Saturday review: a synthesis of the week (exercises + quiz), then the choice between going deeper with your e-Coach (redo the questions you got wrong) or being connected.
